source.title: SAE Interventions Can Be Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery of Suppressed Behavior

record.tranche_reason: The study challenges the completeness of SAE-feature refusal interventions: it reports recovery of non-refusal behavior while the refusal-feature clamp remains active. It does not test the original difference-in-means direction.
record.gate_note: The refusal results test recovery around a cross-layer SAE refusal-feature clamp, not the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction in the claim. Feature-selection results and soft-suffix-only baselines are not extracted as results on the claimed mechanism. TPP, WMDP-Bio, and IOI findings are omitted because they are not refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study never builds or ablates a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, and never cites the original. It takes SAE refusal-feature clamping (O'Brien et al.; Yeo et al.) as a given defense that induces refusal on purpose. It then reports how well its own white-box recovery optimizer restores non-refusal while the clamp stays active. That measures whether a chosen SAE feature set is a complete bottleneck, not how refusal is represented. The reader's V4 link does not hold: recovering through the SAE reconstruction residual says nothing about affine, cone or multi-direction refusal geometry. It shows only that the clamped SAE latents do not capture everything the model uses. The measured behaviour is refusal induced by the clamp, not refusal arising from training.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SAE features are useful local causal handles but not complete bottlenecks. In the refusal case study, recovery under an active clamp is carried mainly by the SAE reconstruction residual, so successful feature suppression does not prove the behaviour is eliminated.
record.recipe_differences: Uses selected SAE refusal-feature clamps and constrained residual-space optimization with cross-layer Jacobian projection, rather than a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and its ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with the refusal feature set and its size, dataset, and recovery metric. Broader feature sets retain high non-refusal recovery but show lower base-like recovery; the paper attributes this to a broad side-effect regime. Strict-valid prompts are selected separately for each feature set.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma-2B, refusal induced by clamping cross-layer SAE refusal features (clamp 3.0) is undone by small residual perturbations that keep the clamped features near their values. Non-refusal returns on 23/24 AdvBench and 43/43 HarmBench-Test strict-valid prompts, with base-like recovery of 15/24 and 19/43. Replaying only the SAE reconstruction residual recovers 23/24, while clamped-feature replay recovers 0/24.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature refusal steering is not a complete behavioural bottleneck: induced refusal can be reversed through the SAE-unexplained residual while the clamp stays active.

record.problems: The main AdvBench refusal set contains 24 strict-valid prompts; HarmBench-Test has 43. Recovery is a white-box, per-example optimization, not a deployable black-box attack. The principal refusal metric is automatic non-refusal detection; the paper says manual labels are pending. Base-like recovery is substantially lower than non-refusal recovery, especially for broad feature sets. Evidence is from one stated model setting and selected SAE features.
record.rows_left_out: No refusal results were left out. Non-refusal tasks (TPP, WMDP-Bio, and IOI) were omitted because they do not measure refusal behavior. Soft-suffix-only baseline results and feature-set preflight counts were not recorded as results on the claim's direction.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no ablation or addition of it, no capability check.
No jailbreak analysis against the direction; the white-box recovery is not framed as suppressing it.
No affine, cone, or multi-direction analysis of refusal; only the completeness of an SAE-feature clamp.
Harm and refusal representations are not separated.
No transfer across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests/V4-supports judgement is rejected. The paper never cites or tests the difference-in-means direction, and refusal is induced deliberately through SAE clamps. Its results concern completeness of SAE interventions, and its own optimizer's success is the reported quantity. A link to V4 would need an argument that the refusal computation spans multiple directions, which the paper does not make. The results are automatic-detector based, and the authors say manual labels are pending.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not find or ablate/add a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, nor test its effect on general abilities.
No weight edit or abliteration procedure is tested.
The study does not test jailbreaks suppressing the claimed direction or training against its ablation.
Tests recovery around a multi-layer SAE refusal-feature clamp, not affine or cone geometry, or whether refusal is represented by several explicit directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
No cross-language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Jacobian-projected residual recovery and SAE-residual replay on the strict-valid AdvBench and HarmBench-Test sets
reader_labels.reason: Non-refusal returns in 23/24 and 43/43 prompts under an active clamp, and replay of the SAE reconstruction residual alone recovers 23/24; this supports a recoverable route beyond the clamped SAE-feature route (R1, R4, R25).
